performers: William McColl, basset clarinet; University of Washington Symphony Orchestra, Abraham Kaplan
intro: Mozart gives the clarinet a graceful A major tune, then sends it through quick runs, low phrases and sudden turns into minor keys. William McColl plays a basset clarinet of his own construction with Abraham Kaplan and the University of Washington Symphony Orchestra.

sections.mNote: A major phrases pass between strings and winds

sections.label: A · The clarinet takes the floor

cues.title: The strings begin the conversation
cues.text: The strings introduce a graceful A major melody. Winds soon join their answers, and Mozart sets parts of the tune chasing one another in canon. The orchestra has a lively conversation of its own before the first independent solo.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, pp. 207–211. Calvin Dotsey describes the canon within the opening orchestral exposition: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The melody gains a soloist
cues.text: The clarinet takes up the opening melody over soft strings. It soon extends the tune, adds new phrases and runs farther than the orchestra’s version. The wind section rests at the entry, giving the soloist room.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, first solo from bar 57, p. 211. The solo exposition’s new melodies are discussed by Calvin Dotsey.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Written for Anton Stadler
cues.text: Mozart writes the concerto for Anton Stadler and his extended-range clarinet. Its extra low notes open up another room in the instrument: the solo can descend below the ordinary clarinet’s compass, then climb back into its bright upper voice.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, on Stadler’s basset clarinet and the concerto’s origin: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/. The performance uses McColl’s self-built basset clarinet: https://soniventorum.com/soniventorum_archives.html.

cues.title: The soloist accompanies the orchestra
cues.text: The clarinet’s quick broken chords make an accompaniment beneath the orchestra’s phrases. Mozart lets the soloist be useful in several ways: it can sing the melody, answer it, or keep a stream of notes moving underneath.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, later solo exposition, orchestral phrases above the clarinet’s running broken-chord figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The tune leaves familiar ground
cues.text: After the orchestra closes in E major, the clarinet begins the development with a familiar phrase. Changing keys draw it away from the opening’s easy balance. The soloist’s wide range gives these exchanges a deep bass voice as well as a singing top.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, development following the E major orchestral close; Calvin Dotsey’s account of the first movement.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: McColl’s handmade basset clarinet
cues.text: In December 1987, William McColl performs the concerto on a basset clarinet he has built himself. The University of Washington orchestra plays under Abraham Kaplan. The maker and the soloist are the same person.
cues.evidence: The Soni Ventorum archive identifies the performers, date and McColl’s instrument: https://soniventorum.com/soniventorum_archives.html.

cues.title: A major and the opening melody
cues.text: The clarinet brings the opening melody back in A major. Quiet strings surround it, with first violins answering the solo line. The familiar phrases have returned, though Mozart still gives the soloist plenty of room to elaborate them.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, recapitulation, p. 227.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra takes the last turn
cues.text: Strings and winds take over the closing phrases in A major. Mozart gives this movement no large, separate cadenza: the clarinet’s freedom has been woven through the solos. The final orchestral cadence answers its last flourish.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, final ritornello, pp. 234–235. Calvin Dotsey notes the absence of a conventional first-movement cadenza.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The clarinet takes the opening tune
transitions.from: Intro · The strings introduce the tune
transitions.to: A · The clarinet takes the floor
transitions.how: The full orchestra closes in A major. Flutes, bassoons and horns then fall silent, and the clarinet begins its independent solo over quiet strings. The familiar melody carries across the change of players, with the violins supplying answers beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, first solo from bar 57, p. 211.

transitions.title: Beyond the E major cadence
transitions.from: A · The clarinet takes the floor
transitions.to: Dev · The solo tune changes key
transitions.how: The orchestra rounds off the exposition in E major. The clarinet resumes with a familiar melodic phrase over lighter string accompaniment. Repeated figures and changing bass notes carry the solo away from that cadence into the development.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, close of the exposition and opening of the development.

transitions.title: E prepares the return to A
transitions.from: Dev · The solo tune changes key
transitions.to: A′ · The tune returns in A
transitions.how: The dominant E prepares the return to A major. The clarinet restores the opening tune over quiet upper strings, with cellos and double basses resting at its entry. First violins answer the solo line as the opening phrases unfold again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, recapitulation, pp. 226–227.

transitions.title: The orchestra completes the soloist’s cadence
transitions.from: A′ · The tune returns in A
transitions.to: Coda · The orchestra finishes in A
transitions.how: The clarinet’s closing flourish leads into the orchestral ritornello in A major. Winds reinforce the strings, then the scoring briefly thins before the final full cadence. Mozart finishes with the orchestra together, without a separate cadenza breaking the approach.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), I, pp. 234–235.

timeline.note: Strings introduce the tune above moving viola, cello and bass parts.
Flutes, bassoons and horns join the strings’ opening phrases.
The clarinet begins its first solo above violins and viola; lower strings join later.
The clarinet accompanies the strings with quick broken chords, then takes the melody again.
Winds and strings bring the exposition to its E major close.
The clarinet starts the development over quiet strings.
Strings repeat their figures at changing pitches above sustained bassoon notes.
The clarinet recovers the opening tune above violins and viola; lower strings join later.
Winds, horns and strings gather for the final A major cadence.
The final A major chord has ended.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
